title: Why a Real Symmetric Matrix Has Real Eigenvalues
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix is a real number.
short: Self-adjointness forces the quadratic form v*Av to equal its own complex conjugate.
long: An eigenvector may initially be complex even for a real matrix, so the proof works over the complexification. Because A equals its conjugate transpose, v*Av is a real number; but it also equals lambda times v*v, and v*v is a positive real, so lambda must be real. The same argument shows eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
consequence: This is the first hint of the spectral theorem and is why covariance matrices, Hessians and other self-adjoint operators have physically interpretable real spectra.

title: The Spectral Theorem
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: A real symmetric matrix can be diagonalised by an orthogonal change of basis.
short: There is an orthonormal basis made entirely of eigenvectors — geometry and algebra line up perfectly.
long: The spectral theorem says more than 'eigenvalues exist': the eigenvectors can be chosen mutually perpendicular and normalised. This turns quadratic forms into sums of squares, gives a canonical picture of conic sections and quadrics, and makes functions of matrices computable by applying them to eigenvalues.
proof: Induct on dimension: a real symmetric matrix has a real eigenvalue and a unit eigenvector; its orthogonal complement is invariant, so repeat there and collect the orthonormal eigenvectors as columns of Q.
consequence: Principal component analysis, the singular value decomposition, and the diagonalisation of the Laplacian on a graph all rest on this result.

title: The Cayley–Hamilton Theorem
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.
short: Substituting a matrix into its own characteristic polynomial gives the zero matrix.
long: This is surprising because the characteristic polynomial is defined through a determinant, yet evaluating it at a matrix is meaningful and yields exactly zero. It lets high powers of a matrix be reduced to a polynomial of degree less than the dimension.
proof: For a diagonalisable matrix evaluate p on its eigenbasis. The general case follows because diagonalisable matrices are dense and matrix multiplication is continuous, or by the adjugate identity (\lambda I-A)\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I-A)=p_A(\lambda)I.
consequence: It simplifies computing matrix exponentials and powers, and is used in control theory and the theory of linear recurrences.

title: The Rank–Nullity Theorem
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The dimension of the image plus the dimension of the kernel equals the dimension of the domain.
short: A linear map either sends a direction somewhere new or collapses it — there is no third option.
long: Choosing a basis of the kernel and extending it to a basis of the whole space, the images of the added vectors form a basis of the image. This reconciles the abstract definition of a linear map with the row-reduction algorithms used in practice.
proof: Extend a basis u_1,\dots,u_k of ker T with vectors v_1,\dots,v_r; then Tv_1,\dots,Tv_r are linearly independent and span im T, so k+r=\dim V.
consequence: It explains why a homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations has a nontrivial solution and underlies the dimension counts in least squares.

title: Similar Matrices Share Their Spectrum
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Change of basis does not change eigenvalues, determinant, trace or characteristic polynomial.
short: Eigenvalues belong to the linear transformation, not to the particular matrix used to write it down.
long: A matrix is a coordinate description of a map. Conjugating by an invertible matrix merely changes coordinates, so intrinsic quantities must be unchanged. This is why the determinant is well-defined on a linear map independently of a basis.
proof: \det(\lambda I-P^{-1}AP)=\det(P^{-1}(\lambda I-A)P)=\det(\lambda I-A) by multiplicativity of determinant.
consequence: It justifies speaking of the eigenvalues of an operator and is the foundation of canonical forms such as Jordan normal form.

title: Cayley's Theorem
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Every finite group is isomorphic to a group of permutations.
short: Group theory is the study of symmetry because every finite group literally acts by rearranging its own elements.
long: Left multiplication by a fixed group element is a bijection of the group onto itself. The map sending g to that permutation is an injective homomorphism, so any finite group embeds in a symmetric group. Abstract finite groups are therefore never more general than permutation groups.
proof: The map is a homomorphism because left multiplication composes as L_g L_h = L_{gh}; it is injective because L_g(e)=g.
consequence: It explains the historical origin of group theory and is the first step in computational group theory, where groups are represented as permutation groups.

title: Lagrange's Theorem
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The order of a subgroup divides the order of the finite group.
short: Cosets partition a finite group into equally sized blocks, so the subgroup size must divide the whole.
long: The left cosets of H all have the same size as H, and any two cosets are either identical or disjoint. Counting the blocks gives the theorem immediately. The converse is false: a divisor of the group order need not be the order of a subgroup.
proof: The map h\mapsto gh is a bijection H\to gH; distinct cosets are disjoint and cover G, so |G| equals the number of cosets times |H|.
consequence: It implies that the order of any group element divides the group order and gives a quick proof of Fermat's little theorem.

title: Classification of Finite Abelian Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Every finite abelian group is a direct product of cyclic groups of prime-power order.
short: A complete, finite invariant exists for abelian groups: once you know the elementary divisors, you know the group.
long: The decomposition is unique up to reordering, giving a full classification. It reduces questions about finite abelian groups to arithmetic with prime powers, and it is the prototype for structure theorems throughout algebra.
proof: Decompose into p-primary components using Bezout identities, then split each component by choosing elements of maximal order and iterating on the quotient.
consequence: It counts the number of abelian groups of a given order and is used in the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups applications to modules and number fields.

title: The Enormity of the Finite Simple Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Every finite group is built from a finite list of simple groups, together with several infinite families.
latex: G\ \text{has a composition series with simple factors}
short: Simple groups are the atoms of finite group theory, and their complete classification took decades.
long: The Jordan–Hölder theorem guarantees that the multiset of simple composition factors is an invariant of a finite group. The classification theorem lists them: cyclic and alternating families, groups of Lie type, and 26 sporadic exceptions including the Monster group.
proof: Existence of composition series follows from finiteness; Jordan–Hölder gives uniqueness of the factor list up to order and isomorphism. The classification itself is a vast body of work spanning thousands of pages.
consequence: It turns many questions about arbitrary finite groups into checks against a finite list, and it revealed deep unexpected connections such as monstrous moonshine.

title: The First Isomorphism Theorem
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Quotienting by the kernel of a homomorphism produces an isomorphic copy of its image.
short: The abstract way of saying that a map becomes bijective once you identify everything it collapses.
long: The theorem unifies the familiar facts that a matrix induces an isomorphism from the row space to the column space, and that modding out by a normal subgroup recovers the target of a homomorphism. It is one of the four isomorphism theorems and appears for groups, rings, modules and vector spaces.
proof: Define \bar\varphi(g\ker\varphi)=\varphi(g); well-definedness, injectivity and surjectivity onto the image all follow immediately from the definition of the kernel.
consequence: It is the standard tool for identifying quotient structures, from Z/nZ to quotient rings in algebraic geometry.

title: The Determinant Measures Volume Scaling
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The absolute value of a determinant is the factor by which a linear map scales oriented volume.
short: A negative determinant also records a reversal of orientation — a mirror reflection in the transformation.
long: For a 2x2 matrix the determinant is the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns; in three dimensions it is a signed volume. This geometric reading explains why singular matrices have determinant zero and why determinants multiply under composition.
proof: Both sides are alternating multilinear functions of the columns and agree on the standard basis, so they agree everywhere.
consequence: Change-of-variables formulas in multivariable calculus use the Jacobian determinant for exactly this reason.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root.
short: The complex numbers are algebraically closed — no polynomial ever needs a larger field to find its roots.
long: The theorem is not really about algebra: every known proof uses some analysis or topology. One proof minimises |p(z)| and shows a minimum with nonzero value can always be decreased; another uses Liouville's theorem applied to 1/p.
proof: If p has no zero then 1/p is entire and bounded (it tends to 0 at infinity), hence constant by Liouville's theorem — contradicting that p is nonconstant.
consequence: It guarantees that an n-th degree polynomial has exactly n roots counted with multiplicity and underpins the spectral theory of matrices.

title: A Rotation Has Complex Eigenvalues
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: A plane rotation by an angle that is not a multiple of pi has no real eigenvalues.
short: Rotating a vector changes its direction, so no real vector can be merely scaled by the map.
long: The characteristic polynomial is lambda^2 - 2cos(theta) lambda + 1, whose discriminant is negative unless sin(theta)=0. Over the complex numbers the eigenvectors appear in conjugate pairs. This is the simplest example of why complex eigenvalues are indispensable even for real matrices.
proof: The discriminant 4(cos^2 theta - 1) = -4 sin^2 theta is negative for theta not a multiple of pi.
consequence: Oscillations, rotations and spiral dynamics are all encoded by complex-conjugate eigenvalue pairs whose modulus governs growth and whose argument governs angular speed.

title: A Basis Is the Same Size in Every Coordinate System
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same number of elements.
short: Dimension is well-defined because a larger spanning set can always be traded against a smaller independent one.
long: The exchange lemma says that if one set spans and another is linearly independent, the independent set cannot be larger. This deceptively simple fact is what makes the word 'dimension' meaningful and allows row rank to equal column rank.
proof: Steinitz exchange lemma: replace vectors of the spanning set one at a time by vectors of the independent set without losing the spanning property, so the independent set has at most as many elements.
consequence: It gives the rank of a matrix as an intrinsic invariant and is used throughout the dimension arguments in algebraic geometry and representation theory.

title: Jordan Normal Form
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Over the complex numbers every matrix is similar to a block diagonal matrix with eigenvalue blocks and ones on the superdiagonal.
short: When eigenvectors are not enough, generalised eigenvectors supply the missing directions.
long: A non-diagonalisable matrix fails to have a full eigenbasis because some eigenspace is too small. Jordan form measures exactly how far from diagonalisable it is: each block of size k contributes one eigenvector and k-1 generalised eigenvectors. It exists over any algebraically closed field.
proof: Decompose the space into generalised eigenspaces using the primary decomposition theorem, then build chains of generalised eigenvectors inside each one.
consequence: It makes computing matrix exponentials and powers explicit, and it classifies similarity over the complex numbers.

title: Galois Theory and the Insolubility of the Quintic
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A polynomial is solvable by radicals exactly when its Galois group is a solvable group.
short: A question about formulas for roots becomes a question about the structure of a permutation group.
long: Galois attached a group to a polynomial by looking at how its roots can be permuted while fixing the coefficients. Radicals correspond to a chain of normal subgroups with abelian quotients. Since the symmetric group on five letters is not solvable, a general quintic has no formula by radicals.
proof: Adjoining an n-th root corresponds to a cyclic extension, so a radical tower gives a subnormal series with abelian factors. The generic polynomial of degree five has Galois group S_5, which is not solvable.
consequence: It settled a centuries-old problem and established a dictionary between field extensions and groups that dominates modern number theory.
